evidence: The association of lactate level with mortality in patients with suspected infection and sepsis is well established [45, 46].
note: Direction and threshold of the lactate-mortality association not given in the input; population is patients with suspected infection and sepsis.

evidence: Its use is currently recommended as part of the SSC Hour-1 sepsis bundle for those patients with sepsis [47, 48], and an elevated lactate is part of the Sepsis-3 definition of septic shock [49].
note: 'Elevated' implies an upper-direction comparison, but no cutoff for the Sepsis-3 septic shock definition is given in the input; lactate is only one part of that definition (other components not stated).

evidence: The lactate cutoffs determining an elevated level ranged from 1.6 to 2.5  mmol/L, although diagnostic characteristics were similar regardless of the cutoff.
note: Cutoffs for 'elevated' lactate varied across studies (1.6-2.5 mmol/L); no single threshold chosen. Used as an adjunctive screening test in adults with suspected but not confirmed sepsis; lactate alone is neither sensitive nor specific enough to rule in or rule out sepsis.
